svg.aria-label: Diagram: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling warm pools. A warm pool is a pool of pre-initialized EC2 instances that sits alongside an Auto Scaling group, and as instances leave the warm pool they count toward the desired capacity of the group, which is known as a warm start. The documentation opens with a warning rather than a recommendation: creating a warm pool when it is not required can lead to unnecessary costs, and if your first boot time does not cause noticeable latency issues for your application there probably is not a need for you to use a warm pool. Sizing is the first surprise. By default the size of the warm pool is calculated as the difference between the Auto Scaling group's maximum capacity and its desired capacity, so with a desired capacity of 6 and a maximum capacity of 10 the warm pool will be 4 when first set up. Maximum capacity is usually headroom reserved for emergency spikes, so the default pool is sized from capacity you never intended to run. The MaxGroupPreparedCapacity option sets the pool ceiling separately, and the documentation's own example is a group of 1,000 instances with a maximum of 1,500 and a warm pool of 100 rather than 500 reserved for future use. There is no minimum size set by default, and MinSize statically sets the minimum number of instances to maintain. Three pool states are available: Stopped, Running or Hibernated. Keeping instances Stopped is an effective way to minimize costs, where you pay only for the volumes that you use and the Elastic IP addresses attached to the instances. Hibernated stops instances without deleting their memory contents, saving RAM to the EBS root volume, and while instances are in hibernation you pay only for the EBS volumes including storage for the RAM contents and the Elastic IP addresses. Keeping instances in a Running state inside the warm pool is also possible but is highly discouraged to avoid incurring unnecessary charges. The critical interaction is with lifecycle hooks. Auto Scaling stops or hibernates instances as they enter the warm pool and does not wait for user data to finish running, so the stop or hibernate action can interrupt long-running user data. In a warm pool configuration lifecycle hooks delay instances from being stopped or hibernated and from being put in service during a scale-out event until they have finished initializing, and if you add a warm pool without a lifecycle hook, instances that take a long time to finish initializing could be stopped or hibernated and then put in service during a scale-out event before they are ready. A feature bought to make instances ready sooner can therefore serve traffic from instances that are less ready. Scale-in behaviour is configurable: by default Auto Scaling terminates instances when the group scales in and then launches new instances into the warm pool to replace them, while an instance reuse policy returns instances to the warm pool instead; if instances do not meet the hibernation requirements they fall back to being stopped instead of hibernated. Other behaviours worth knowing: while instances are in the warm pool, scaling policies only scale out if the metric value from instances in the InService state exceeds the policy's alarm high threshold; if the warm pool is depleted during a scale-out event instances launch directly into the group, a cold start; an instance that fails to reach InService is considered a failed launch and terminated regardless of the underlying cause; an instance refresh replaces InService instances first and then warm pool instances; warm pools are not supported with weighted mixed instance groups; and an instance can only be stopped or hibernated if it has an EBS volume as its root device.
svg.title: The default warm pool is sized from capacity you never meant to run
svg.text: The docs open by telling you that you probably do not need this.
“Creating a warm pool when it’s not required can lead to unnecessary costs. If your first boot time does
not cause noticeable latency issues for your application, there probably isn’t a need…”
Default size = max − desired, and max is your emergency headroom
“By default, the size of the warm pool is calculated as the difference between the Auto Scaling group’s
maximum capacity and its desired capacity.”
desired 6, max 10 → pool of 4. desired 1000, max 1500 → pool of 500 unless capped.
Three states, and what each one bills
Stopped volumes you use + Elastic IPs · “effective way to minimize costs”
Hibernated EBS incl. RAM contents + Elastic IPs · keeps memory, restores on start
Running the full instance · “highly discouraged”
MaxGroupPreparedCapacity caps the pool. MinSize floors it — there is no default minimum.
Without a lifecycle hook, the pool can serve traffic from a half-built instance
“Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling stops or hibernates instances as they enter the warm pool, and does not wait
for user data to finish running.”
“… instances that take a long time to finish initializing could be stopped or hibernated and then put in
service during a scale-out event before they are ready.” A hook is what prevents it.
SCALE IN: TERMINATE OR REUSE
Default: terminate, then launch new ones
into the pool to replace them
Instance reuse policy returns them instead
Not hibernation-eligible? Falls back to stopped.
WHEN THE POOL DOES NOT HELP
Depleted pool → launch straight into the
group: a cold start
Failed to reach InService → terminated,
“regardless of the underlying cause”
Scaling policies ignore the pool: they scale out only on the metric from instances in the InService state.
No weighted mixed groups, no Spot in mixed groups, and an EBS root volume is required to stop or hibernate at all.
An instance refresh replaces InService instances first, then the pool — so a new AMI reaches the pool last.
